sentences.text: Like other long-necked sauropods, this animal possessed a small skull, sturdy legs, and an extremely long tail. Its build was slightly less robust than that of Apatosaurus, featuring much longer neck vertebrae that created a proportionally longer neck.
The WDC DMJ-021 specimen reveals that the creature had a thickened neck and a deep chest supported by wide ribs, resembling the anatomy of Apatosaurus.
Michael Benton agreed that a specific vertebra from the BYU 9024 collection belongs to this genus, suggesting the animal could reach a length of 50 meters.
Mass estimates for the known specimens range from 35 to 44 metric tons.
Supersaurus is among the largest diplodocids and is possibly the longest sauropod known from well-preserved remains.
Despite unreliable dating methods, the 'Jimbo' specimen is considered possibly the oldest known dinosaur.
The type species, Supersaurus vivianae, was first discovered by Vivian Jones in Colorado in 1972 at the Dry Mesa Quarry.
The genus was formally described by James A. Jensen in 1985, though the name had been used informally since 1973.
The initial discovery consisted of a few bones, including a 2.4-meter-long scapulocoracoid holotype and some neck vertebrae found in the Morrison Formation.
A more complete specimen nicknamed 'Jimbo' was later discovered in Converse County, Wyoming.
Jensen originally described a giant sauropod he named Ultrasaurus macintoshi, which was subsequently renamed Ultrasauros macintoshi based on a dorsal vertebra cataloged as BYU 9044.
The type species of the genus Supersaurus is Supersaurus vivianae, and the genus has had several synonyms including Dystylosaurus, Ultrasauros, Dinehirosaurus, and Jensenosaurus.
The name Ultrasauros is now considered a junior synonym of Supersaurus because Supersaurus was named first, and the genus Dystylosaurus is also now considered a junior synonym.
The parent group of Supersaurus is Diplodocinae, and it belongs to the family Diplodocidae.
Supersaurus lived in North America during the Late Jurassic period, approximately 155.7 to 150.8 million years ago, in what is now North America and possibly Europe.
The fossils of Supersaurus date between 153 and 145 million years ago, specifically from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages, between 154.8 and 143.1 million years ago.
There are 5 recorded fossil occurrences of Supersaurus in the Paleobiology Database.
